title: Chapter 59: Fold It Small, Part 1 of 5: Ro's Letter
html:
Lyra counted the steps of the crypt before it was light.
Twenty-three. From the stone floor at the bottom to the door at the top. She had counted them on the first night she came here, seven days ago, with the snow coming down through the grating and her father far away in the reeds of the north on a barge. She had counted them every morning since. Twenty-three. They had always been twenty-three.
She did not know why that should make her want to put her head down on the cold stone and howl.
She did not. She sat on the bottom step, in her mother's gray gown, with Silas's old black coat over it because there was nothing else, and her knees drawn up, and her hands round her knees, and counted them again. One. Two. Three. Up into the dark. Twenty-three. And then down again. Twenty-three. Twenty-two.
Behind her, in the crypt, the brazier had burned down to a low red glow. Everybody was asleep. Silas in his chair by the steps, with his long legs stretched out and his chin on his chest. Juno curled on the blankets with her whistle. Oren against the far wall, sitting up, with his sword across his knees, asleep with his eyes half open the way old soldiers sleep. Gideon against his father's side by the fire, with his father's great gray hand in his lap. And Big Gideon, sitting where Gideon had put him, against the pillar, with his pale eyes open on nothing. He did not sleep. Lyra did not think he knew how any more.
And Corin.
She did not look at him.
She had looked at him a great deal yesterday. She had not been able to stop. On the roof, and in the crypt, and while Silas wrapped his black fingertips in white linen. While he lay on the floor with her father's evening on his forehead and her hands round his. While he told her everything, in front of all of them, in his flat careful Ministry voice, about the sea coming into a harbor at high tide.
She was not going to look at him this morning. She had decided that in the night. If she did not look at him, she would not see him look back at her the way he looked at Mrs. Doyle, or at the arches. Politely. Kindly. A man looking at a stranger in a crypt.
Are you hurt, miss?
She counted the steps again.
One. Two. Three.
She had known it would cost something. On the floor of the dome, when she saw him lift his hands. She had known it at once. She had seen enough of him, in the autumn and the winter, burning his little things one by one to make a light or a wind, the word for his mother, three winters, his first tongue, to know what it would take to hold that. She had known what was big enough. She had known, while she ran across the floor pulling people out from under it, that she was spending him. And she had gone on running. Because he had bought it, and she would not waste it.
She would do it again.
That was the thing she could not get past, sitting on the step in the dark. She would do it again. If she were back on that floor, now, with the dome coming down and the girl with her mask in her lap and the porters climbing out of the hole, and him on his knees with his hands up, she would do exactly the same. She would not run to him. She would run to them.
And he would do the same. He would burn her again.
She did not know if that made it better or worse.
Five. Six. Seven.
At the top of the steps, the door moved.
Lyra stopped counting.
It was not the wind. It opened slowly, a hand's width, and then wider, and a gray light came in round it, the very first gray of the morning. And a shape stood in it. Not tall. Round. In a long coat with a cape on the shoulders, and a hat with a wide brim pulled down against the cold.
"Miss Lyra?" said a voice. Very low. "Miss Lyra, are you there?"
She knew the voice.
She was up the steps before she knew she had moved. Twenty-three of them. She did not count. And at the top, in the gray doorway, in the cold, with the snow behind him on the churchyard and the dark bulk of a carriage at the lych gate with two gray horses steaming in the shafts, was Tibbs.
Old Tibbs. Thirty years the Thorne groom. Bald under the wide hat, and red-faced, and short, and round. Who had driven her mother out onto the salt flats eleven years ago at a walk, for two hours, and never told anybody. Who had driven her to the Bourse two nights ago in the Duke's dark blue carriage, and waited.
He looked at her. At the burned gown, under Silas's coat. At her hair.
"Oh, miss," said Tibbs.
"I'm all right."
"Oh, Miss Lyra."
"I'm all right, Tibbs. I'm out. We all got out." She did not say not all of us. She did not say Saul. She did not say he doesn't know me. "What is it? Why are you here? Is it the Duke?"
"No, miss." Tibbs took off his wide hat, and held it against his chest, in both hands, the way he held it in church. "It's Master Rowan."
Lyra went very still.
"He came to the mews," said Tibbs. "At Marrow House. At the fourth bell this morning, on foot, in the dark, from your aunt's. On his own. And he banged on the door of my room over the stables till I woke. And he gave me this." He reached inside his coat. "And he said, Take it to her, Tibbs. Wherever she is. Now. Before it's light. And don't let anybody see you. And then he went away again. Back up the Hill. Running." Tibbs held out a letter. "He was white as milk, miss. I never saw him like that. Not even when he was little."
Lyra took the letter.
It was folded in three. Not small. In three, the ordinary way, the way you fold a letter to go in a coat pocket. It was sealed with plain black wax and nothing pressed into it. And on the outside, in a hand she knew, a hand she had not seen for two years, a quick tall untidy hand that went uphill at the end of every line:
L.
That was all.
She stood in the doorway of Saint Bride's in the first gray of the morning and looked at it.
Two years. Two years since she had seen that hand. Since the autumn their father went quiet, and Aunt Cressida came and took Rowan away to the house on the Crescent, and Rowan went, and did not write. Not once. Not when she wrote to him. Not when she went to the house on the Crescent and stood on the step and rang, and the footman said Master Rowan is not at home to you, miss. Not when she sent him the letter by Juno, folded in three, with everything in it. Their father. The barge. The Bourse. Ro. Please.
And then a note, some days ago, by Juno's grandfather's key, slipped under a door. Three lines.
I will not come up.
I have one question.
R.
That was all he had sent. In two years. And she had not known what the question was.
She broke the black wax with her thumb. The cut one. It opened again, and bled a little, and she did not notice.
"Thank you, Tibbs," she said. "Go home. Go back to the Duke. Don't let anybody see you."
"Miss—"
"Go home, Tibbs."
He looked at her a moment longer. Then he put his hat back on, and went down the path through the snow to the lych gate, and climbed up onto the box of the carriage, and shook the reins. And the two gray horses leaned into the collars, and the carriage went away down the lane toward the river, very quietly, with the snow muffling the wheels.
Lyra sat down on the top step, in the open door, in the cold. And unfolded her brother's letter.
It was one page. Written fast. The lines went uphill, the way they always had, and the ink was blotted in two places, as if he had been writing with the pen held too hard.
L.
I read your letter. All of it. Eight times. I didn't answer. You know why. Or you don't. I don't know any more what you know.
I said I had one question. I've been trying to work out how to ask it ever since. I'm just going to write it.
The Inquisitor came to Aunt C.'s on Sunday. To see her. In the morning room. They talked for an hour with the door shut. I was in the library next door and I heard their voices but not the words. And when he went, he left his case on the hall table for a minute while Barrow fetched his coat, and it was open, and there was a book in it.
L., it was ours.
It was the family book. Green cloth. The tree and the crown on the front, in gold thread. And under it, in silver thread, small, the words. You know the words. Mother stitched them. I watched her do it, the winter before she went, by the fire in the nursery, with her feet on the fender. I was seven. I remember the needle going in and out. I remember her saying them over and over while she stitched, under her breath, like a song.
It was on our desk in Father's study for nine years. On the left-hand corner, by the lamp. Every day. I used to trace the letters with my finger when he wasn't looking. And then after Father went quiet it wasn't there any more. I asked Aunt C. She said it must have been put away. I asked Bertram. Bertram said he didn't know. Bertram always knows.
And on Sunday it was in the Inquisitor's case.
He came back for it. He saw me looking. He didn't say anything. He just closed the case, and looked at me, and lifted his hat, and went.
That's my question, L. That's the only one I've got.
Why does the Inquisitor have Mother's book?
R.
P.S. Father is at the Inquisitor's own house. Not a nurse's. Not the Health's. His. On Steeple Lane, at the top of the Hill, behind the Spire. The gray one with no knocker. I heard Aunt C. say it to Barrow when she thought I'd gone up. She was crying. I've never heard her cry.
P.P.S. Don't come to the Crescent. They're watching it.
P.P.P.S. I'm sorry. For the two years. I'm sorry.
Lyra read it twice.
Then she folded it again. In three. The ordinary way. And held it in her lap, on the top step of Saint Bride's, in the gray morning, with the snow on the churchyard and the dark lane going down to the river.
Why does the Inquisitor have Mother's book?
She knew the words. Of course she knew them. They had been on the corner of her father's desk her whole life, in silver thread on green cloth, under the tree and the crown. She had traced them with her finger too. When she was small, and he was not looking, and when she was not small, and he was.
And yesterday afternoon, in this crypt, a man who did not know her had lain on the floor with her father's last evening on his forehead and her hands round his, and come back, and told her what a visitor with a folded face had said to her father in the study on the last night.
Because the dark is the day with its eyes shut, my lord.
Hers. Isolde's.
Lyra sat on the step and did not move.
Then she got up, and went down the twenty-three steps into the crypt, counting, and woke Oren.
"We're going up the Hill," she said. "Now. This morning. In daylight. By the front door."
Oren looked up at her out of his half-open soldier's eyes. And then past her. At the man asleep against the pillar by the dying fire, with a book in his lap and white linen on his black fingertips.
"And him?" said Oren.
Lyra did not look round.
"He said not by myself," she said. "He wrote it down."
Up the Hill
They went at the second bell of the morning. Three of them.
Silas did not want them to go. He said so, standing at the top of the twenty-three steps with his crooked spectacles and his tired face, in his shirtsleeves in the cold. He said Corin could not walk to the end of the lane, never mind up the Hill. He said Oren's shoulder would come out again if he so much as lifted his sword. He said every Watchman in the city had Lyra's face on a paper in his pocket. He said all of it very quietly and very fast, the way a man says a thing he knows will not be listened to.
Then he went down into the crypt and came back up with Corin's crutch.
It was the ash crutch he had made for him the week before, in the arches. Pale wood, worn smooth at the top where Corin's armpit went and at the grip where his hand went. Corin took it in his gray hands, with the white linen on the black fingertips, and looked at it the way he looked at everything now. As if it belonged to somebody else, and he was minding it.
"Thank you," he said.
"Don't thank me," said Silas. "Come back."
And then he gave Lyra a pair of gloves. His own. Old black leather, too big for her, worn through at one fingertip. "For your hands," he said. "They're cut. And for his." He gave Corin another pair. Gray wool, knitted, the kind a carter wears. "Over the linen. Nobody looks twice at a man in wool gloves in winter. Everybody looks twice at gray hands."
Juno wanted to come. Lyra said no. Juno said she was the only one of them who could climb. Lyra said there would be nothing to climb. Juno said there was always something to climb. Lyra said no, in the voice her mother had used, the one that ended things. And Juno looked at her, and then sat down on the top step with her whistle in her fist and her frostbitten feet in their sacking and did not say anything else. But her face said a great deal.
Gideon did not ask to come. He was sitting by the fire with his father. He looked up as they went, and lifted one white curled hand, and let it fall.
So it was three of them.
Lyra went first. Then Oren, with his sword on his hip and his left arm in its sling of Mrs. Fitch's black shawl, and his hat pulled down. Then Corin, on the crutch. Slowly.
She counted.
She always counted. She had counted since she was nine, and she did not know why, and now she did. Count them. Every day. Keep them safe. Her mother's voice. On the bottom stair, in the gray gloves, in the dark blue cloak. She knew why now. It did not make her stop. It made her count harder.
So she counted the steps down Saint Bride's Lane to the river. Two hundred and twelve. The lane was steep and narrow and cobbled and full of old snow gone gray with ash, and Corin came down it a step at a time, with the crutch first and the stiff leg swinging, and Oren beside him, not touching him, ready to. She walked ahead and did not look back. She counted. She heard the crutch on the cobbles behind her. Tap. Swing. Tap. Swing. Two hundred and twelve.
Lantern Bridge. Ninety-one paces. The lamps along it were still burning, in the daytime. Blue. The Crescent Gas. Nobody had come to put them out. There was ash on the glass of them, and on the stone parapet, and on the black water underneath, going slowly down to the sea. Halfway across, Lyra stopped and looked back up the river. Toward the Exchange.
There was a hole in the sky there.
That was how it looked, from the bridge, in the gray morning. Where the dome of the Memory Bourse had stood above the roofs, like a moon coming up behind a hill, there was nothing. A gap. And in the gap, a thin gray smoke still going up, very straight, very slow, into the still air. Like a single thread pulled out of a piece of cloth.
She looked at it for a moment.
Corin had stopped beside her. Leaning on the crutch, breathing hard. He was looking at it too.
"Was it beautiful?" she said. "Before. The dome. From inside. I never looked up. I was looking at the floor."
He was quiet for a moment.
"Yes," he said. "From Cinder Lane. With the light in it. Like a lantern."
"I never saw it from outside. Not lit."
"No," said Corin. "You were inside."
She waited for him to say something else. You were inside, and I came back in for you. He did not. He did not know that. He did not know that he had come back in for her. He only knew it from the book.
She walked on.
The city was strange that morning.
It was quiet. That was the first thing. Not empty. There were people in the streets. More than usual, even, for the second bell on a winter morning. Standing about. In twos and threes. On corners. In doorways. On the steps of churches. Not going anywhere. Just standing. Talking to each other in low voices, the way people talk after a death. And looking north and west, toward the hole in the sky.
Lyra heard them as she passed.
"—saw it from my window, clear as day, a great white light—"
"—and I remembered my mother's kitchen. Just for a minute. The blue jug on the shelf. I'd not thought of that jug in thirty years—"
"—my boy's face. My boy that died. I'd lost his face. I couldn't bring it back, not for years, and last night—"
"—the Inquisitor, they say. They say he did it. They say he went in with a hundred men and set the lamps off on purpose—"
"—they say the Lady's dead. They say she died in her bed at the second bell, with the whole place burning round her—"
"—they say a man held the roof up. On his hands. A man on his knees, with his hands up, holding the whole dome—"
Lyra did not look round. She did not look at Corin. She kept walking, and counting.
Behind her, the crutch went on. Tap. Swing. Tap. Swing. It did not stop. It did not slow down.
Up from the river. Through the Old Town, where the streets were narrow and leaned together. Past the end of Ferrule Street, where there was a small crowd outside a house with an old oil lamp over the door, and a black Ministry carriage, and two men in brown coats carrying something out on a stretcher under a gray blanket. Lyra did not stop. She did not know whose house it was.
Corin stopped.
She heard the crutch stop behind her. She turned round.
He was standing at the end of Ferrule Street, leaning on the crutch, looking down it at the house with the oil lamp and the carriage and the stretcher. And his face had gone very still.
"What is it?" she said.
"The Lamplighter's Rest," said Corin.
He did not say anything else. He did not have to. She knew the name. It was in her own head, not only in his book. The Lamplighter's Rest. Ferrule Street. Linus Hale lives there. Room six. At the top.
The men in brown coats put the stretcher into the back of the black carriage. And shut the doors. And the carriage drove away, up the Old Town toward the Ministry, not fast.
Corin watched it go.
Then he turned and went on, up the hill, with the crutch. And did not say anything. And Lyra did not ask.
The Hill began at the top of Coopers' Lane.
You could tell where it began. The streets got wider. The cobbles got smoother. The houses stood back from the road behind iron railings and little front gardens, white with snow, with clipped dark bushes in them like sentries. The snow on the pavements had been swept. Not by the people who lived there. By other people, early, before anybody who lived there was awake.
And the lamps.
On the Hill, the Crescent Gas lamps stood every thirty paces, on tall iron posts, black, with a curl of iron at the top like the head of a fern. And every one of them was burning. In the day. Blue. Cold. Steady. A long double line of cold blue lights going up the wide swept streets of the Hill ahead of them, in the gray morning, through the falling ash, like a row of candles at a funeral.
Nobody had put them out.
Nobody ever put them out, on the Hill. Lyra knew that. She had grown up under them. They were never put out. They burned day and night, winter and summer, year after year, and nobody ever came to fill them or trim them or light them. They just burned. Clean and blue and steady and always.
She had never once wondered what they burned.
She walked under them now, up the swept pavement, between the iron railings, and counted them. One. A child's summer afternoon. Two. A father's hand. Three. A wedding, whose not known. Four. A boy called Ned, who forgot how to swallow.
She stopped counting the lamps.
At the corner of the Crescent, where the long curve of tall pale houses swept round the top of the Hill, there were two Watchmen. Dark blue coats. Brass buttons. Tall hats. Staves. Standing on the corner, by a lamp, stamping their feet in the cold. One of them was young, with a red nose. One of them was older, with gray whiskers.
The older one saw her.
Lyra saw him see her. Saw his eyes go to her face, under the hood of Silas's old coat, and stop. Saw his hand go to the pocket of his dark blue coat. Where the paper would be. Wanted. The Thorne Abduction. Saw him take it half out, and look at it, and look at her.
She did not stop walking.
She walked straight toward him. Up the swept pavement, under the burning blue lamps, with Oren behind her and Corin behind Oren. She walked the way her mother had walked into a room. Not fast. Not slow. As if the room had been waiting for her and had better be ready.
The older Watchman stepped out in front of her.
"Miss," he said. "Miss Thorne."
"Yes."
The young one with the red nose stared at her with his mouth open.
The older one looked at the paper in his hand. And at her. And at the paper. And then, slowly, he folded it up, and put it back in his pocket.
"The Inquisitor said you might come," he said. "This morning. Up the Crescent. By daylight." He did not look at Oren, or at Corin. He looked at her. "He said if you came, we were to let you through. You and whoever was with you. And not to follow." He stepped back out of her way. "Steeple Lane, miss. Behind the Spire. The gray house. You'll know it."
Lyra looked at him.
Then she walked past him, without a word, and round the corner of the Crescent, and up toward the Spire.
Behind her, she heard the young Watchman say, in a whisper, "Was that her? Was that the one? With the—"
And the older one say, "Shut up, Nat."
And the crutch, coming after her. Tap. Swing. Tap. Swing.
The Spire stood at the very top of the Hill. She had always known it. Everybody in Veridia knew it. You could see it from the river, from the Saltmarsh, from the far end of Lantern Quay. A single tower of white stone, very tall, very thin, going up into the sky like a needle, with no windows in it at all except at the very top, where there was a ring of tall narrow openings like the slots in a dovecote. The Choir sang there. Every day. At the second bell after noon. You could hear it from the Crescent, on a still day, coming down from the top of the Spire. High and sweet and very clear. Children's voices.
The Choir gets first choice of the quiet young ones.
Lyra did not look up at the Spire as she went past the foot of it.
Behind it, there was a lane. Narrow. Steep. Going down a little way off the top of the Hill, between high garden walls, toward the back of the Spire. Cobbled. Not swept. Old snow on it, gray with ash, unmarked except for one line of footprints going down and one coming back.
And at the end of the lane, where it stopped against a wall, a house.
It was gray. Plain gray stone, three stories, narrow, with plain gray shutters, all shut. No railings. No front garden. No clipped bushes. No lamp. Five plain stone steps up to a plain dark door with no knocker on it. Not even the four holes where a knocker had been. Just the door. Plain. Shut. Waiting.
It was the plainest house Lyra had ever seen on the Hill.
She stood at the bottom of the five steps and looked at it.
Oren came and stood beside her. Then Corin, on the crutch, breathing hard, his face gray under the wool cap Silas had pulled down over his ears.
Nobody said anything.
Then Lyra went up the five steps, and lifted her hand in Silas's old black glove, and knocked on the Inquisitor's door. Three times. And then twice.
She did not know why she knocked it like that.
She only knew that she had.
